prompt: What does it mean that Vue is a "progressive framework"?
explanation: Vue is progressive: you can drop it into a page for a single interactive widget, or scale up to a full single-page application with a build tool — adopting only what you need.

options.text: It only works with the newest browsers
You can adopt it incrementally — from one widget via a CDN up to a full build-tool app
It automatically upgrades your code to new versions
It must always be used with a backend server

prompt: Which style does this course use for writing component logic?
explanation: Both the Options API and the Composition API are fully supported, but this course uses the Composition API with <script setup>, the recommended default for new projects.

prompt: Which of these are blocks in a single-file component (.vue file)? Select all that apply.
explanation: An SFC bundles <template> (HTML), <script>/<script setup> (logic), and <style> (CSS). There is no <database> block.

prompt: Vue automatically tracks which data the UI depends on and updates the DOM when it changes. This system is called ______. (one word)
explanation: Reactivity is the system that tracks data usage and re-renders the affected part of the UI when the data changes.

prompt: Why can't a .vue single-file component run directly in the browser without tooling?
explanation: The .vue SFC format is compiled by a build tool (Vite) into standard JavaScript and CSS. The CDN build instead uses plain JavaScript component objects, which need no compilation.

options.text: Browsers block .vue files for security reasons
SFCs must be compiled by a build tool like Vite into JavaScript the browser can run
SFCs only work on the server
They actually do run directly in every browser

prompt: Match each term to its description.
explanation: Declarative rendering is the core idea; the Composition and Options APIs are the two logic styles; an SFC is the .vue file format that holds all three blocks.

pairs.right: Describe the UI for a state; Vue updates the DOM
Logic built from functions like ref and computed
Logic grouped into data/methods/computed options
A .vue file with template, script, and style

prompt: What does createApp(App).mount('#app') do?
explanation: createApp builds an application instance from the root component, and .mount('#app') attaches and renders it onto the matching DOM element.

options.text: Creates an app from the root component and renders it into the #app element

prompt: Which is the correct way to bind an element's href to a `url` variable?
explanation: Mustaches don't work in attributes. Use v-bind, whose shorthand is a colon: :href="url".

prompt: When should you avoid v-html?
explanation: v-html renders a raw HTML string, so untrusted content can inject scripts (cross-site scripting). Use it only with trusted, sanitized HTML.

options.text: Whenever the HTML comes from users or untrusted sources (XSS risk)
Only when the page is in dark mode

prompt: A template attribute that starts with `v-` and applies reactive behavior is called a ______. (one word)
explanation: Directives (v-bind, v-on, v-if, v-for, v-model, …) are special v-prefixed attributes that apply reactive behavior to the DOM.

prompt: Which statements about template bindings are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: Interpolation renders text, @ is the v-on shorthand, and null/undefined removes a bound attribute. Bindings accept a single expression, not a statement like an if.

options.text: {{ }} inserts a value as plain text
A binding can contain a full if-statement
Binding a value of null or undefined removes the attribute

prompt: In `v-on:click.prevent="onSubmit"`, match each part to what it is.
explanation: A directive has a name (v-on), an optional argument after the colon (click), optional modifiers after dots (prevent), and a value expression (onSubmit).

pairs.right: Directive name
Argument
Modifier
Value (the expression)

prompt: How do you read the current value of `const count = ref(0)` inside a <script> block?
explanation: In JavaScript you access a ref's inner value through .value (count.value). In templates, top-level refs are auto-unwrapped so you write count.

prompt: In a template, how do you display `const count = ref(0)`?
explanation: Templates automatically unwrap top-level refs, so {{ count }} shows the value — no .value needed.

prompt: Which statements about reactive() are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: reactive works only on collection types, is deep, but breaks if you reassign the whole object. Destructuring its properties DISCONNECTS them from reactivity.

options.text: It only works on objects, arrays, Map, and Set
Destructuring its properties keeps them reactive
Reassigning the whole object breaks reactivity
It provides deep reactivity for nested properties

prompt: To make a single number reactive, you should use ______(0) rather than reactive(0). (name the function)
explanation: reactive only works on objects, so a primitive number must use ref(0).

prompt: Why does a ref use a .value wrapper instead of just being a plain variable?
explanation: JavaScript can't detect access to a plain variable. Wrapping the value in an object lets Vue define a getter/setter on .value and observe every read and write.

options.text: To make the code longer on purpose
So Vue can intercept reads and writes of .value to track and trigger reactive updates
Because JavaScript requires all variables to have a .value
To store the value on a server

prompt: Which is the recommended default for reactive state, and why?
explanation: ref is the recommended default: it works for primitives and objects, can be reassigned through .value, and doesn't lose reactivity when destructured or passed around.

options.text: ref, because it holds any type, can be reassigned via .value, and survives being passed around
Plain variables, because they are simplest
It doesn't matter; they behave identically

prompt: What is the key advantage of a computed property over a method for derived values?
explanation: A computed caches its result based on its dependencies and re-runs only when one of them changes; a method runs every time it is called.

options.text: It is cached and only re-evaluates when a reactive dependency changes
It can perform side effects safely
It never needs to be read

prompt: When does a computed property re-run its getter?
explanation: Vue tracks which reactive values the getter reads and re-evaluates only when one of those dependencies changes.

options.text: Only when one of its reactive dependencies changes

prompt: How do you make a computed property writable?
explanation: computed({ get, set }) creates a writable computed; assigning to its .value calls the setter.

options.text: You can't — computed is always read-only
Pass computed() an object with get and set functions

prompt: A computed getter should be free of ______ effects — it should only derive and return a value. (one word)
explanation: Computed getters must be side-effect-free; mutating other state or fetching data belongs in a watcher, not a getter.

prompt: Which are good reasons to use a computed property? Select all that apply.
explanation: Computed properties name and cache derived values from reactive state. They must not perform side effects like fetching data.

options.text: To keep the template clean by naming a derived value
To cache an expensive calculation over reactive data
To run a fetch request each time it's read
To derive a value from other reactive state

prompt: You call a computed property's value 10 times without changing its dependencies. How many times does the getter actually run?
explanation: The getter runs once and the cached result is reused until a dependency changes.

prompt: What is the main difference between v-if and v-show?
explanation: v-if truly creates or destroys the element and is lazy; v-show keeps the element in the DOM and just toggles display, making it cheaper to flip frequently.

options.text: v-if toggles CSS display; v-show adds/removes the element
v-if adds/removes the element (and is lazy); v-show only toggles the CSS display property
v-show only works on the server

prompt: Why should each v-for item have a stable, unique :key?
explanation: The key is a stable identity for each item, letting Vue track items across changes and reuse DOM nodes instead of rebuilding them — preventing subtle state bugs.

options.text: It's required syntax or the loop won't run
So Vue can match items across updates and reuse/reorder DOM nodes correctly

prompt: In Vue 3, what happens if you put v-if and v-for on the same element?
explanation: In Vue 3, v-if takes priority over v-for on the same element, so the loop variable isn't available to the condition. Filter with a computed property instead.

options.text: v-for runs first, so v-if can filter each item
v-if has higher priority and runs first, so it can't access the loop variable

prompt: To filter a list before rendering it, do the filtering in a ______ property and loop over the result. (one word)
explanation: Filtering and sorting belong in a computed property; then v-for iterates over the derived list — avoiding the v-if/v-for pitfall.

prompt: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: v-else must be adjacent; index-as-key breaks on reorder; and <template> groups elements without a real DOM node. v-show does NOT remove the element — it sets display: none.

options.text: v-else must immediately follow a v-if (or v-else-if) element
Using the array index as key is risky for lists that reorder
v-show removes the element from the DOM when false
You can put v-if or v-for on a <template> to group elements without an extra wrapper

prompt: Order these from cheapest to most expensive to TOGGLE repeatedly (visibility on/off many times).
explanation: v-show only flips a CSS property, so it's cheap to toggle repeatedly. v-if creates and destroys the element (and its components/listeners) each time, which costs more per toggle.

prompt: What does :class="{ active: isActive }" do?
explanation: In the object syntax, each key is a class name toggled by the truthiness of its value — 'active' applies when isActive is truthy.

options.text: Applies the 'active' class only when isActive is truthy

prompt: If an element has both class="card" and :class="{ selected: isSelected }", what happens?
explanation: Static class and dynamic :class merge, so 'card' is always present and 'selected' is added conditionally.

options.text: The dynamic class replaces the static one
They merge — 'card' is always applied, 'selected' when isSelected is truthy
Only the static class is used

prompt: Which is a correct :style binding for a dynamic pixel font size?
explanation: Style values are expressions, so you must include the unit: size + 'px'. Property names use camelCase (fontSize) or quoted kebab-case.

prompt: Vue automatically adds vendor ______ to CSS properties that need them, so you write the standard property name. (one word)
explanation: Vue auto-prefixes styles requiring vendor prefixes at runtime, so you don't have to write them manually.

prompt: Which are valid ways to use :class? Select all that apply.
explanation: class binding supports object syntax, array syntax, and objects nested in arrays. A bare number is not a meaningful class binding.

options.text: An object nested inside an array: :class="[base, { active: isActive }]"

prompt: When should you prefer toggling a CSS class (:class) over inline :style?
explanation: Prefer :class for reusable/themable styles. Use :style for values computed from state, like a width percentage or a dynamic color.

options.text: Never — inline styles are always better
For reusable or themable styling; reserve :style for values genuinely derived from state

prompt: What does @submit.prevent="save" do on a form?
explanation: The .prevent modifier calls event.preventDefault() for you, so the browser doesn't reload the page, and then your save handler runs.

options.text: Prevents the form from ever submitting
Calls event.preventDefault() and then runs save, stopping the default page reload

prompt: What is the difference between @click="save" and @click="save()"?
explanation: @click="save" passes the function reference; @click="save()" invokes save during render (and uses its return value), which is usually a mistake unless you intend to pass arguments.

options.text: @click="save" uses the function as the handler; @click="save()" calls it immediately at render

prompt: To collect several checkboxes into one value, what should you bind them to with v-model?
explanation: Bind multiple checkboxes to the same array with v-model; each checked box's value is added to the array. A single checkbox bound to a boolean is for on/off.

prompt: The v-model modifier that trims leading and trailing whitespace is .______ (one word).
explanation: v-model.trim removes surrounding whitespace from the bound value; .number casts to a number and .lazy syncs on change.

prompt: v-model on a text input is essentially shorthand for what?
explanation: For a text input, v-model binds :value to the state and listens for the input event to write changes back — two-way binding.

options.text: Binding :value and updating state on the input event

prompt: Which are valid event modifiers in Vue? Select all that apply.
explanation: .prevent, .stop, and key modifiers like .enter are real. There is no .reload modifier.

prompt: Which lifecycle hook runs once the component's DOM exists, making it the right place for initial data fetching or DOM access?
explanation: onMounted runs after the component is inserted into the DOM, so template refs are available and it's a natural place to fetch initial data.

prompt: How does watchEffect differ from watch?
explanation: watchEffect runs its function right away and re-runs when any reactive value it read changes. watch is lazy, takes explicit sources, and provides old and new values.

options.text: watchEffect runs only on the server
watchEffect runs immediately and auto-tracks reactive state it reads; watch is lazy with explicit sources

prompt: Where should you clean up a timer or event listener that you set up in onMounted?
explanation: Pair setup with cleanup: tear down timers, listeners, and subscriptions in onUnmounted so they don't leak after the component is removed.

options.text: You don't need to clean it up

prompt: By default, a watcher callback runs BEFORE the DOM updates. To run it AFTER the DOM updates, set flush to '______'. (one word)
explanation: The default flush is 'pre' (before DOM update). Use flush: 'post' when the callback needs to read the updated DOM.

prompt: Why must lifecycle hooks be called synchronously inside setup (not inside an if or after await)?
explanation: Hooks register callbacks against the active component instance during setup. Calling them conditionally or after an await can break that association.

options.text: So Vue can associate them with the current component instance; otherwise they may fail to register

prompt: Match each tool to its typical job.
explanation: onMounted/onUnmounted bracket setup and cleanup; watch reacts to an explicit source; watchEffect auto-tracks whatever it reads.

pairs.right: Fetch data / access the DOM after mount
Clean up timers and listeners
React to a specific source with old + new values
Keep something in sync with the state it reads

prompt: In a <script setup> SFC, what do you need to do to use a child component in the template?
explanation: With <script setup>, importing a component registers it locally, so you can use its tag directly without a components: option.

options.text: Register it in a components: option
Import it in <script setup> — that's enough

prompt: What does <script setup> expose to the template?
explanation: All top-level bindings declared in <script setup> are automatically available to the template; there is no return statement.

options.text: Every top-level binding (refs, functions, computeds, imported components), with no return statement

prompt: Does a Vue 3 component template require a single root element?
explanation: Vue 3 allows multiple root elements in a template, so a single wrapper element is optional.

options.text: No — Vue 3 supports multiple root nodes (fragments)

prompt: By convention, Vue component names are written in ______Case (e.g. UserCard). (one word, the case name)
explanation: Components are named in PascalCase, matching the imported name and typically the file name.

prompt: Which statements about components are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: Components are reusable, each instance is independent, and apps are trees of them. In <script setup>, a child MUST be imported to be used.

options.text: Each use of a component is an independent instance with its own state
Components let you reuse UI and logic
A child component works in <script setup> without being imported
Apps are typically built as a tree of components

prompt: How does a parent pass data down to a child component?
explanation: Parents pass data to children via props — custom attributes on the component tag (covered in depth in the next lesson).

options.text: Through props (attributes on the component tag)
By modifying the child's internal state directly

prompt: Is defineProps imported from 'vue'?
explanation: defineProps (like defineEmits and defineModel) is a compile-time macro handled by the SFC compiler — you use it without importing it.

options.text: No — it's a compile-time macro available in <script setup>

prompt: How do you give type-based props default values?
explanation: The withDefaults helper adds default values to type-based props: withDefaults(defineProps<T>(), { size: 'md' }).

options.text: You can't have defaults with the type-based form

prompt: Can a child component change the value of a prop it receives?
explanation: Props follow one-way data flow and are read-only in the child. To change parent-owned data, emit an event; for an editable value, copy the prop into local state.

options.text: No — props are read-only; emit an event or copy to local state to change data
Only if the prop is a number

prompt: What is the difference between likes="42" and :likes="42" on a component?
explanation: A plain attribute passes a literal string; v-bind (:) evaluates the expression, so :likes="42" passes the number 42.

options.text: likes="42" passes the string "42"; :likes="42" binds the expression, passing the number 42

prompt: Props flow in ______ direction(s) — parent to child — and are read-only in the child. (a number word)
explanation: This is one-way data flow: data flows one direction, down from parent to child, and props are read-only.

prompt: A child needs an editable value seeded from a prop. What's the correct approach?
explanation: Since props are read-only, copy the prop into a local ref for the child to edit (and use a watcher if it must re-sync when the prop changes).

options.text: Copy the prop into a local ref and edit that

prompt: How does a child component send data up to its parent?
explanation: Children emit events; the parent listens with @eventName and updates its own state. Mutating props is not allowed (one-way data flow).

options.text: By emitting a custom event (declared with defineEmits) that the parent listens to with @event
By editing the parent's variables directly

prompt: What does a default v-model on a component desugar to?
explanation: By default, v-model on a component maps to a modelValue prop plus an update:modelValue event. defineModel wires this up automatically.

options.text: A value prop and a change event
A modelValue prop and an update:modelValue event
A ref stored on the parent only

prompt: Since which Vue version is the defineModel macro stable?
explanation: defineModel became stable in Vue 3.4, simplifying two-way component bindings.

prompt: The compile-time macro used to declare the events a component can emit is define______. (complete the word)
explanation: defineEmits declares a component's events (with optional TypeScript payload types) and returns the emit function.

prompt: How do you expose a named model for v-model:title on a child?
explanation: const title = defineModel('title') creates a named model that the parent binds with v-model:title. A component can expose several named models.

prompt: Match each mechanism to what it's for.
explanation: Props go down, emits go up, defineModel creates two-way v-model, and update:modelValue is the event behind a default v-model.

pairs.right: Pass data down to a child
Send events (data) up to the parent
Two-way binding via v-model
The event a default v-model listens for

prompt: What do slots let a parent pass into a child that props cannot?
explanation: Props pass data values; slots pass template markup, letting the parent supply content that the child renders in a <slot> outlet.

prompt: What is the content written between <slot>…</slot> tags?
explanation: Content inside a <slot> is fallback content; it renders only if the parent doesn't fill that slot.

options.text: Fallback content, shown only when the parent provides nothing for that slot

prompt: How does a parent fill a named slot called "footer"?
explanation: The parent uses <template #footer> (shorthand for v-slot:footer), which fills the child's <slot name="footer">.

prompt: Why can't ordinary slot content read the child's internal variables?
explanation: Slot content lives in the parent's scope. To expose child data, use a scoped slot: the child binds data on <slot :item="x" /> and the parent receives it.

options.text: Because slot content is compiled in the parent's scope, not the child's
Because variables are private in JavaScript

prompt: A slot that passes data from the child to the slot content is called a ______ slot. (one word)
explanation: Scoped slots expose slot props from the child, so the parent can render child-owned data (like each item in a list).

prompt: You want a reusable list component that iterates items internally but lets the parent decide how each row looks. What do you use?
explanation: A scoped slot lets the child own iteration while exposing each item to the parent, which supplies the row markup — the ideal pattern for flexible list/renderer components.

options.text: A scoped slot exposing each item

prompt: What problem do provide and inject solve?
explanation: provide/inject lets an ancestor share data directly with any descendant, avoiding the need to thread a prop through every layer in between.

options.text: Prop drilling — passing data through many intermediate components that don't use it

prompt: To share reactive state via provide, what should you provide?
explanation: Provide the ref/reactive itself so injectors stay reactive. Providing count.value hands over a one-time snapshot that won't update.

options.text: The ref's unwrapped value, e.g. count.value
The ref (or reactive object) itself, e.g. count

prompt: What is the second argument to inject(key, default) used for?
explanation: The optional second argument is a fallback value returned when the key wasn't provided anywhere up the tree.

options.text: A default value used if no ancestor provided that key

prompt: For type-safe injection in TypeScript, use an Injection______ (a typed Symbol) as the key. (one word)
explanation: An InjectionKey<T> is a Symbol typed to carry the value's type, so provide/inject are type-checked.

prompt: How can you let descendants read shared state but not directly mutate it?
explanation: Wrapping the state in readonly() before providing prevents descendants from reassigning it; provide separate functions to make controlled changes.

options.text: Provide it wrapped in readonly() and expose functions for controlled updates

prompt: When is a Pinia store a better fit than provide/inject?
explanation: provide/inject shines for a subtree's context; app-wide state that many unrelated components share is usually cleaner in a Pinia store.

options.text: For a single value shared within one subtree
For app-wide shared state used across many unrelated parts of the app

prompt: What is a composable in Vue?
explanation: A composable is a reusable function, conventionally named useX, that packages reactive state and behavior using the Composition API.

options.text: A function (named useX) that uses the Composition API to encapsulate and reuse stateful logic
A special kind of component tag

prompt: Two components call the same composable that declares its state inside the function. Do they share that state?
explanation: State created inside the composable is per-call. To share one instance across the app, declare the state at module scope (outside the function).

options.text: No — each call creates its own independent state

prompt: How does a composable make components share a single state instance?
explanation: Module-scoped state (declared outside the useX function) is created once and shared by every caller — a lightweight store pattern.

options.text: By declaring the reactive state at module scope, outside the function

prompt: By convention, a composable's name starts with the word ______. (one word)
explanation: Composables are named useX (useMouse, useFetch, useCounter) by convention.

prompt: Why did composables replace mixins? Select all that apply.
explanation: Composables avoid mixins' name collisions and unclear origins; you see the imports and returned names and can rename on destructure. Mixins are not server-only.

options.text: With mixins it was unclear which mixin a property came from
Composables make the source of each value explicit and renamable
Mixins only work on the server

prompt: Where should a composable put its event-listener cleanup?
explanation: A composable registers onUnmounted internally; the hook belongs to whichever component called it, so cleanup happens automatically on unmount.

options.text: Nowhere — Vue never cleans up listeners
In an onUnmounted hook inside the composable, so it runs for the calling component

prompt: What does <RouterView> do?
explanation: <RouterView> is the outlet where Vue Router renders whichever component matches the current route.

options.text: Renders the component matched by the current URL

prompt: How do you read a dynamic route parameter :id inside a component?
explanation: useRoute() returns the current route; its params object holds dynamic segments, e.g. route.params.id.

prompt: Why should you use <RouterLink> instead of a plain <a href> for internal navigation?
explanation: RouterLink handles the click to navigate within the SPA without reloading the page; a plain <a href> triggers a full reload.

options.text: It navigates client-side without a full-page reload
Plain <a> tags don't work in Vue

prompt: With createWebHistory (clean URLs), the server must serve index.html for unknown paths — a so-called SPA ______. (one word)
explanation: History mode needs a SPA fallback so deep-link refreshes serve index.html instead of 404ing. Hash mode avoids this.

prompt: What is a navigation guard like router.beforeEach used for?
explanation: Guards run before a route change; returning false cancels it and returning a location redirects — commonly used to protect authenticated routes.

options.text: Running logic (e.g. auth checks) before a navigation completes, to allow, cancel, or redirect it

prompt: Order these steps to set up Vue Router.
explanation: Define routes, create the router with a history mode, register it on the app with app.use, then render matched components with <RouterView>.

prompt: What are the three core parts of a Pinia store?
explanation: A Pinia store has state (reactive data), getters (cached derived values), and actions (methods that change state, possibly async).

prompt: Why use storeToRefs when destructuring a store?
explanation: Like destructuring a reactive object, pulling state/getters off a store copies values and breaks reactivity. storeToRefs preserves it; actions can be destructured directly.

options.text: Destructuring state/getters directly loses reactivity; storeToRefs returns them as reactive refs

prompt: What is Pinia's relationship to Vuex?
explanation: Pinia is the official, recommended state library for Vue and the successor to Vuex, which is in maintenance.

options.text: Pinia is a plugin for Vuex
Pinia is the officially recommended successor to Vuex, which is now in maintenance mode

prompt: You define a Pinia store with the function define______('id', ...). (complete the word)
explanation: defineStore(id, setupOrOptions) creates a store; you then use it via the returned useXStore() function.

prompt: Which state is the best fit for a Pinia store rather than a local ref?
explanation: Pinia shines for genuinely app-wide shared state (user, cart, theme). Component-only data belongs in a local ref.

options.text: A counter used by one component only
The logged-in user, needed by many unrelated components across the app
A temporary value inside a single function

prompt: Which statements about Pinia are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: Actions may be async, getters are cached like computed, and Pinia must be installed with app.use. A store is shared and can be used anywhere.

options.text: Actions can be async (e.g. fetch data then set state)
Getters are cached, like computed properties
You must register Pinia with app.use(createPinia())
A store can only be used in one component

prompt: When is a template ref populated with its DOM element?
explanation: Template refs are null during setup and are filled once the element is mounted, so you access them in onMounted or later.

options.text: After the component mounts (e.g. in onMounted)

prompt: How does a <script setup> child let a parent call one of its methods via a ref?
explanation: <script setup> components are closed by default; defineExpose declares which properties/methods are visible to a parent's component ref.

options.text: It's automatic — all methods are public
The child declares the method with defineExpose

prompt: You change state and immediately need to read the updated DOM. What do you await?
explanation: Vue batches DOM updates; awaiting nextTick() resolves after those updates are applied, so the DOM reflects your latest state.

prompt: To destructure a reactive object without losing reactivity, wrap it with to______. (complete the word)
explanation: toRefs converts each property of a reactive object into a linked ref, so destructured values stay reactive.

prompt: What does toValue(x) do that unref(x) does not?
explanation: unref returns x.value for a ref (else x). toValue additionally invokes x when it's a getter function — ideal for MaybeRefOrGetter inputs in composables.

options.text: It also calls x if x is a getter function, not just unwrapping a ref

prompt: If you put ref="item" on an element inside a v-for, what does the ref hold?
explanation: A ref used inside v-for collects the rendered elements into an array whose order matches the list.

options.text: An array of the elements, in list order

prompt: What JavaScript feature powers Vue 3's reactivity for objects?
explanation: Vue 3 uses Proxies: reads are tracked and writes trigger dependent effects to re-run. (Vue 2 used Object.defineProperty.)

options.text: Proxies (with get/set traps that track and trigger)

prompt: What does shallowRef track?
explanation: shallowRef reacts to .value being reassigned but not to deep mutations of the held object; use triggerRef to force an update after a deep change.

options.text: Only reassignment of its .value, not deep mutations

prompt: What is customRef used for?
explanation: customRef gives you track and trigger functions so you decide exactly when the ref records a dependency and notifies effects — perfect for debounce/throttle.

options.text: Creating a ref with custom control over when it tracks and triggers (e.g. a debounced ref)

prompt: To flag an object so Vue never makes it reactive, wrap it with mark______. (complete the word)
explanation: markRaw prevents an object from being converted into a reactive proxy — useful for third-party instances or large inert data.

prompt: You deeply mutate a shallowRef's held object and the UI doesn't update. What's a correct fix?
explanation: shallowRef only reacts to .value reassignment, so either reassign .value or call triggerRef to force dependent effects to re-run.

prompt: Match each reactivity tool to its purpose.
explanation: shallowRef limits depth, customRef customizes timing, toRaw unwraps a proxy, and markRaw opts an object out of reactivity entirely.

pairs.right: Track only top-level .value reassignment
Custom control of track/trigger (e.g. debounce)
Get the original non-proxied object
Prevent an object from becoming reactive

prompt: What does <Teleport to="body"> do?
